profile.reading:
KOMO Plaza, known for most of its history as Fisher Plaza, is a broadcast and technology complex in the Lower Queen Anne neighborhood of Seattle, within sight of the Space Needle. The site's roots trace back to the Fisher family, who founded KOMO radio in 1926 and put KOMO-TV on the air in 1953, building the family's Fisher Communications into one of the Pacific Northwest's most established broadcasters. Fisher Communications owned and operated the plaza that bears its stations' call letters for decades, before Sinclair Broadcast Group acquired the company in 2013 for roughly 373.3 million dollars and took over the Seattle properties, including this complex, which was subsequently renamed KOMO Plaza.

This registry entry, KOMO Plaza East, denotes one of two adjacent structures at the site, standing roughly 30 to 40 meters from its counterpart, KOMO Plaza West. Complexes built to house television and radio broadcast operations of this scale routinely include not just studios and newsrooms but the technical infrastructure that keeps a broadcaster on air around the clock: master control rooms, transmission equipment, server rooms for newsroom and production systems, and increasingly the networking and storage infrastructure that supports digital and streaming operations alongside the over the air broadcast. It is that technical backbone, rather than a commercial colocation business, that puts a facility like this on a registry of data center infrastructure.

The complex has had a notable history beyond routine broadcast operations. A serious electrical fire broke out at the plaza on July 2, 2009, an incident significant enough to be documented in retrospectives of the building's history. In March 2014 a television news helicopter crashed near the complex. More recently, after Sinclair purchased several Seattle radio stations in September 2021, those stations, operating under the Lotus brand, also took up residence at KOMO Plaza rather than relocating elsewhere, underscoring the site's continued role as a hub for Seattle broadcast operations under Sinclair ownership.

No public source distinguishes a separate street address, floor plan, or technical specification for the East structure apart from the West, and Sinclair Broadcast Group, as a broadcasting conglomerate rather than a data center operator, does not publish facility-level detail of the kind a colocation provider would. What is documented is the plaza's identity, ownership history, and continuous use as an active broadcast and technology site in the heart of Seattle.

reading.body:
KOMO Plaza East is a multi-use facility in Seattle's Lower Queen Anne neighborhood that shares a single street address with an adjacent building, KOMO Plaza West, roughly 30 to 40 meters apart. The facility is operated by Sinclair Broadcast Group, a telecommunications conglomerate, as part of a complex formerly known as Fisher Plaza. No power capacity, IT load, or cooling specifications are published for this site.

Without published specifications, this campus cannot be assessed for relevance to AI infrastructure scaling. The research note indicates this registry entry may represent a wing or section of a shared commercial complex rather than a distinct data center facility, and the absence of any power figures distinguishes it from the two other Washington state facilities with published capacity.

Washington state has 46 mapped data center facilities, but only two publish power specifications, totaling 60 MW. This campus ranks third by published megawatts in the state, a ranking that reflects no published figure rather than a measured capacity.
